newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Chip stocks surge in Asia on firmer prices.
newsitem.headline: Chip stocks surge in Asia on firmer prices.

text.p: Boosted by signs that sliding chip prices have stabilised, semiconductor-related shares rose in South Korea and Japan on Friday although profit-taking took some Taiwan issues lower, traders said.
Also buoying the market were good overnight gains by chip makers in the United States, helped by Wall Street's rise past the 7,000 barrier for the first time.
Samsung Electronics, the world's leading memory chip maker, rose 500 won to 59,500. It briefly hit its daily high of 61,000.
LG Semicon was up 1,600 won to its daily limit-up 22,700, and Hyundai Electronics climbed 2,200 won to its limit of 30,200.
Industry analysts said spot prices for the 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips were around $10 per unit, up from $6-$8 a month ago.
Production cuts announced by Samsung Electronics and LG Semicon were factors in the rising prices, they said.
"Chip prices are likely to strengthen for the time being," said Koo Hee-jin, an analyst at the Daishin Economic Reserch Institute.
Brokers said while the price of memory chips could fluctuate for some time, those stocks remained undervalued.
"Given the deep consolidation shares went through last year when chip prices plunged about 80 percent, semiconductor shares are undervalued," said Choo Hee-yup, a broker at Donwon Securities.
Samsung dropped to a low of 38,600 won in January from an all-time high of 173,000 won in October, 1995, before rebounding.
In Tokyo, shares in Tokyo Electron Ltd, which makes semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, jumped to the highest level for this financial year, closing 140 yen higher at 4,530.
But Taiwan's recently hot electronic shares fell sharply as profit-taking gripped the sector.
Taiwan Semiconductor, the island's top chip maker, lost T$2.50 or 3.94 percent to T$61 on heavy trade volume of 35.1 million shares.
Brokers said investors largely ignored recent news that prices for 16-megabit DRAMs had rebounded.
"Taiwan's chip companies have already risen on that piece of news. It is nothing new to the market," said Chen Han-chung, analyst for Yungli Securities.
